# Worksheet: adding a latent period

**~45 minutes**

The [chapter](../chapters/05-jump-processes.qmd) simulated an SIR epidemic as an
exact sequence of events: draw a waiting time, pick which event fires, update the
state, repeat. Here you keep that process and change the *disease*. Many
infections have a **latent period**, someone infected but not yet infectious,
which adds a fourth compartment $E$ and a third transition.

You will not write the simulation loop. You will *describe the events* and let
`JumpSystem` build the process for you, then run many realisations at once with
an `EnsembleProblem`.

**How to use this file.** Run cells one at a time with `Ctrl+Shift+Enter`. Cells
marked `# TODO` have a line or two for you to complete; everything else runs as
given. Each part ends with `✓` / `✗` lines that check your answer; a `✗` is
information, not failure, and the collapsed hint below it will get you moving.
An instructor is circulating; ask early rather than staying stuck.

**Parts A and B are the session.** **Part C** goes further if you get there; not
reaching it is fine. Worked solutions are posted at the end of each
day. Run `git pull` to collect them.

**New to Julia?** The
[Julia essentials worksheet](01-julia-essentials-for-modelers.qmd)
opens with an R-to-Julia table, and the
[Julia essentials chapter](../prerequisites/01-julia-essentials.qmd) has the
full one.

::: {.callout-note}
The next session writes these same transitions as a reaction network and
generates this jump process, an ODE and a moment approximation from one
description of the flows. You are not being asked to judge which is better yet;
today is about simulating the events exactly.
:::

## Greek letters you can copy

`\gamma` followed by `Tab` gives `γ` at a Julia prompt, but that completion
often does not fire inside a Quarto file like this one. Copy what you need
from here, or insert it from the command palette with the Unicode Latex
extension described in [Setting up](../setup.qmd#optional-extras).

| Symbol | Reads as | At a Julia prompt |
|---|---|---|
| `β` | beta | `\beta` then `Tab` |
| `γ` | gamma | `\gamma` then `Tab` |
| `κ` | kappa | `\kappa` then `Tab` |
| `σ` | sigma | `\sigma` then `Tab` |
| `₀` | subscript zero | `\_0` then `Tab` |

A subscript is its own character too: `R₀` is `R` followed by `₀`.

Plain ASCII names work exactly as well if you prefer them.
:::

## Setup

Run this and check `R₀` prints as 2.0.

`@variables` and `@parameters` create *symbols*, not numbers: `S` is the name of
a compartment, and the numbers arrive later when you build a problem.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch04-setup
using ModelingToolkit
using JumpProcesses
using CairoMakie
using StableRNGs
using Statistics
using ModelingToolkit: t_nounits as t

check(name, condition) =
    println(condition ? "✓ $name" : "✗ $name — not right yet, see the hint")

@parameters κ σ γ
@variables S(t) E(t) I(t) R(t)

κ_value = 0.05 * 10 / 1000   # β c / N, as in the session
σ_value = 0.5                # progression rate: mean latent period 1/σ = 2 days
γ_value = 0.25               # recovery rate
grid = 0.0:0.5:120.0
tspan = (0.0, last(grid))

println("R₀ = ", 0.05 * 10 / γ_value)
```

---

## Part A — an exposed compartment (~15 min)

The disease now has three transitions rather than two:

| transition | who moves | propensity |
|---|---|---|
| infection | $S \to E$ | $\kappa SI$ |
| progression | $E \to I$ | $\sigma E$ |
| recovery | $I \to R$ | $\gamma I$ |

A `MassActionJump` describes one transition with **two lists**, and the
difference between them is the whole idea:

- the **reactant** list says who has to be *present* for the event, and so sets
  the propensity: `[S => 1, I => 1]` means the rate is $\kappa \cdot S \cdot I$;
- the **net** list says what the event *does* to the state: `[S => -1, E => 1]`
  moves one person out of $S$ and into $E$.

Recovery is done for you as a worked example. Fix the other two.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch04-a1
# Present for the event -> propensity        What the event does to the state
infection = MassActionJump(κ,
    [S => 1],                                # TODO: who else must be present?
    [S => -1, E => 1];
    scale_rates = false)

progression = MassActionJump(σ,
    [E => 1],
    [E => -1, R => 1];                       # TODO: where does an exposed person go?
    scale_rates = false)

recovery = MassActionJump(γ,                 # worked example: I --> R at rate γI
    [I => 1],
    [I => -1, R => 1];
    scale_rates = false)

@named seir = JumpSystem([infection, progression, recovery], t,
                         [S, E, I, R], [κ, σ, γ])
seir_system = complete(seir)

# One map carries both the initial state and the parameter values.
seir_start = [S => 990, E => 0, I => 10, R => 0,
              κ => κ_value, σ => σ_value, γ => γ_value]

seir_problem(seed; start = seir_start) =
    JumpProblem(seir_system, start, tspan; rng = StableRNG(seed))

solution = solve(seir_problem(1), SSAStepper(); saveat = grid)

# A second run with nobody infectious: if the propensity is right, nothing at
# all can happen, because infection needs an infectious person present.
quiet = solve(seir_problem(2; start = [S => 1000, E => 0, I => 0, R => 0,
                                       κ => κ_value, σ => σ_value, γ => γ_value]),
              SSAStepper(); saveat = grid)

check("population conserved",
      all(solution[S] .+ solution[E] .+ solution[I] .+ solution[R] .== 1000))
check("nobody went negative", minimum(minimum(solution[x]) for x in (S, E, I, R)) >= 0)
check("infection needs an infectious person present", all(quiet[S] .== 1000))
check("exposed individuals go on to become infectious", maximum(solution[I]) > 10)
check("an epidemic happened", solution[R][end] > 100)
println("peak infectious = ", maximum(solution[I]),
        ", ever infected = ", solution[R][end])
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint — Part A

```julia
infection = MassActionJump(κ, [S => 1, I => 1], [S => -1, E => 1]; scale_rates = false)
progression = MassActionJump(σ, [E => 1], [E => -1, I => 1]; scale_rates = false)
```

Infection is the only transition that needs *two* people: one susceptible to
infect and one infectious to do the infecting. That is why its propensity is a
product, and why `I` belongs in the reactant list even though infection does not
change `I` — an infectious person is unchanged by infecting someone.

Progression moves a person from $E$ to $I$, not from $E$ to $R$; skipping
straight to recovered would mean nobody new ever becomes infectious.

`scale_rates = false` says the rate constant is already the propensity
coefficient, with no combinatorial factor applied. Every reaction here involves
one individual of each species, so there is nothing to scale.
:::

### A1. Interpret

Why is the first propensity a product of two compartments while the other two
depend on only one?

Then look again at the two lists in each `MassActionJump`. Why does `I` appear
in the reactant list of `infection` but not in its net list, and what would go
wrong if you moved it?

> *Your answer here.*

## Part B — does the latent period matter? (~15 min)

One realisation tells you very little. A stochastic model has to be run many
times — the *same* model with the *same* parameters, differing only in the
random stream — and an `EnsembleProblem` says that in three lines instead of a
loop you write yourself.

`prob_func` builds the problem for trajectory `ctx.sim_id`, which is where each
run gets its own seed. Without it every trajectory would share one random
stream, which is a real trap once the runs are threaded.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch04-b0
seir_ensemble = EnsembleProblem(seir_problem(100);
    prob_func = (prob, ctx) -> seir_problem(100 + ctx.sim_id))

seir_runs = solve(seir_ensemble, SSAStepper(), EnsembleThreads();
                  trajectories = 30, saveat = grid)

peaks = [maximum(r[I]) for r in seir_runs.u]

check("thirty runs came back", length(seir_runs.u) == 30)
check("the runs differ from each other", std(peaks) > 0)
println("peak infectious over 30 runs: mean ", round(mean(peaks); digits = 1),
        ", sd ", round(std(peaks); digits = 1))
```

Note what did *not* change: the model, the parameters, the solver. Only
`trajectories` says how much simulation you want, so asking for 3000 instead of
30 is a one-character edit rather than a rewrite.

To compare two models you also need them on a common time grid, which the
trajectories do not otherwise share — each one stops at its own last event.
`EnsembleSummary` does that reduction, and `summarise` below is just the three
lines above with the model left as an argument.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch04-b1
sir_start = [S => 990, I => 10, R => 0, κ => κ_value, γ => γ_value]

@named sir = JumpSystem(
    [MassActionJump(κ, [S => 1, I => 1], [S => -1, I => 1]; scale_rates = false),
     MassActionJump(γ, [I => 1], [I => -1, R => 1]; scale_rates = false)],
    t, [S, I, R], [κ, γ])
sir_system = complete(sir)

sir_problem(seed) = JumpProblem(sir_system, sir_start, tspan; rng = StableRNG(seed))

function summarise(make_problem, seed0; trajectories = 30)
    ensemble = EnsembleProblem(make_problem(seed0);
                               prob_func = (prob, ctx) -> make_problem(seed0 + ctx.sim_id))
    runs = solve(ensemble, SSAStepper(), EnsembleThreads();
                 trajectories = trajectories, saveat = grid)
    return EnsembleSummary(runs, grid)
end

seir_summary = summarise(seir_problem, 100)
sir_summary = summarise(sir_problem, 200)

# summary.u holds the mean state at each grid point; row order follows the
# unknowns of the system, so I is row 3 for SEIR and row 2 for SIR.
seir_mean = reduce(hcat, seir_summary.u.u)
sir_mean = reduce(hcat, sir_summary.u.u)
seir_I, sir_I = seir_mean[3, :], sir_mean[2, :]
seir_final, sir_final = seir_mean[4, end], sir_mean[3, end]

check("the SEIR peak comes later", grid[argmax(seir_I)] > grid[argmax(sir_I)])
check("the SEIR peak is lower", maximum(seir_I) < maximum(sir_I))
check("both reach a similar final size",
      abs(seir_final - sir_final) / sir_final < 0.05)
(; seir_peak_day = grid[argmax(seir_I)], sir_peak_day = grid[argmax(sir_I)],
   seir_peak = round(maximum(seir_I); digits = 1),
   sir_peak = round(maximum(sir_I); digits = 1),
   seir_final = round(seir_final; digits = 1),
   sir_final = round(sir_final; digits = 1))
```

This compares your Part A model with a plain SIR, so it stays ✗ until the two
jumps above are right.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ws-ch04-compare
#| fig-cap: "Mean infectious curve over 30 exact simulations, with and without a latent period, with the 5th-95th percentile band for the SEIR model (the `EnsembleSummary` default)."
seir_low = reduce(hcat, seir_summary.qlow.u)[3, :]
seir_high = reduce(hcat, seir_summary.qhigh.u)[3, :]

fig = Figure(size = (720, 400))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "time (days)", ylabel = "mean infectious")
band!(ax, grid, seir_low, seir_high; color = (:steelblue, 0.2))
lines!(ax, grid, sir_I; color = :firebrick, linewidth = 3, label = "SIR")
lines!(ax, grid, seir_I; color = :steelblue, linewidth = 3, label = "SEIR")
xlims!(ax, 0, 70)
axislegend(ax; position = :rt)
fig
```

### B1. Interpret

- Approximately when does each epidemic peak, and roughly how much lower is the
  SEIR peak?
- Both models end with about the same number of people ever infected, but the
  curves look very different. What does the latent period change, and what does
  it leave alone?
- The shaded band is wide near the peak and narrow at the start. Why?

> *Your answer here.*

### B2. Experiment

Try a shorter and a longer latent period either side of the baseline
$\sigma = 0.5$, and watch the peak move.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch04-b2
latent_rates = Float64[]   # TODO: fill this list — try σ = 1.0, 0.5, and 0.25

for s in latent_rates
    start = [S => 990, E => 0, I => 10, R => 0,
             κ => κ_value, σ => s, γ => γ_value]
    summary = summarise(seed -> seir_problem(seed; start = start), 300;
                        trajectories = 10)
    mean_I = reduce(hcat, summary.u.u)[3, :]
    println("mean latent period ", round(1 / s; digits = 1), " days → peak on day ",
            grid[argmax(mean_I)])
end

check("three latent periods tried", length(latent_rates) == 3)
```

Does doubling the latent period move the peak by twice as much, or by more?

> *Your answer here.*

## Part C — how often does an outbreak fizzle out? (optional)

*Start this only if you have finished Part B.*

Every simulation so far began with 10 infectious people and every one produced
an epidemic. Real introductions are usually a single case, and many single cases
infect nobody. A deterministic model cannot describe this at all; an exact
event simulation can.

The quantity to compare against is $1/R_0$, but be clear about where it comes
from. While cases are few the susceptible pool is essentially undepleted, so an
infectious individual infects at rate $\beta c$ and recovers at rate $\gamma$:
a linear birth–death process. Because infectious lifetimes are exponential
here, its extinction probability is $q = \gamma/(\beta c) = 1/R_0$ when
$R_0 > 1$. That formula belongs to this approximation; it is not universal
across branching processes or infectious-period distributions.

Two further approximations separate it from what the code measures. This model
has 999 susceptibles, not infinitely many, and the code below scores an outbreak
as faded if fewer than 20 people were ever infected rather than asking whether
transmission stopped. The run is a check on how good an approximation
$1/R_0$ is here.

Here `output_func` earns its place: each trajectory is reduced to a single
`true`/`false` the moment it finishes, so 400 full paths are never held in
memory at once.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch04-c1
single_case = [S => 990, E => 0, I => 10, R => 0,      # TODO: start from ONE infectious individual
               κ => κ_value, σ => σ_value, γ => γ_value]

# Outcomes are bimodal: a handful of cases, or hundreds. Any cut between the
# two modes gives the same answer, so 20 is not a delicate choice.
fade_ensemble = EnsembleProblem(
    seir_problem(5000; start = single_case);
    prob_func = (prob, ctx) -> seir_problem(5000 + ctx.sim_id; start = single_case),
    output_func = (sol, ctx) -> (sol[R][end] < 20, false))

trials = 400
faded = solve(fade_ensemble, SSAStepper(), EnsembleThreads(); trajectories = trials)
fade_fraction = count(faded.u) / trials
predicted = γ_value / (0.05 * 10)   # 1 / R₀, the branching-process approximation

infectious_at_start = only(x.second for x in single_case if isequal(x.first, I))
check("started from a single infectious individual", infectious_at_start == 1)
check("fade-out is close to the branching prediction",
      abs(fade_fraction - predicted) < 0.05)
(; fade_fraction, predicted)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint — Part C

```julia
single_case = [S => 999, E => 0, I => 1, R => 0,
               κ => κ_value, σ => σ_value, γ => γ_value]
```

Keep the population at 1000: one infectious individual means 999 susceptible
ones. If the fraction comes out near zero, check you did not leave 10 infectious
people in the starting state.
:::

- What fraction of outbreaks died out, and how does it compare with $1/R_0$?
- The deterministic model, started from one case, predicts a certain epidemic
  every time. Why can it not produce the answer you just measured?
